_link.title: I can explain the role of ADH in regulating water reabsorption and how this connects the excretory and endocrine systems

options.text: Antidiuretic hormone
Adrenaline-derived hormone
Anti-dehydration hormone
Adrenal-dependent hormone

explanations.a: Correct. ADH stands for antidiuretic hormone. 'Antidiuretic' means it works against the production of dilute urine (diuresis).
explanations.b: Incorrect. ADH is not derived from adrenaline. It is produced by the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary.
explanations.c: Incorrect. While ADH helps prevent dehydration, the correct full name is antidiuretic hormone.
explanations.d: Incorrect. ADH is released from the posterior pituitary, not the adrenal gland.

options.text: The posterior pituitary gland
The thyroid gland
The adrenal cortex
The pancreas

explanations.a: Correct. ADH is released from the posterior pituitary gland into the bloodstream.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The thyroid gland produces thyroxine and calcitonin, not ADH.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The adrenal cortex produces cortisol and aldosterone, not ADH.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The pancreas produces insulin and glucagon, not ADH.

toLevel2.stem: Which parts of the nephron does ADH act on to increase water reabsorption?

options.text: The distal tubule and collecting duct
The glomerulus and Bowman's capsule
The proximal tubule only
The ascending loop of Henle

explanations.a: Correct. ADH increases the water permeability of the distal tubule and collecting duct, allowing more water to be reabsorbed by osmosis.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The glomerulus and Bowman's capsule are the site of filtration, which is not regulated by ADH.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The proximal tubule performs bulk reabsorption that is not regulated by ADH.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The ascending loop of Henle is impermeable to water and is not a target of ADH.

toLevel2.stem: What triggers the release of ADH from the posterior pituitary?

options.text: A rise in blood osmolality (solute concentration)
A drop in blood glucose levels
An increase in body temperature
A rise in blood oxygen levels

explanations.a: Correct. When blood becomes more concentrated (higher osmolality), such as during dehydration, the posterior pituitary releases more ADH.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Low blood glucose triggers insulin regulation, not ADH release.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Body temperature is regulated by other mechanisms; ADH specifically responds to blood solute concentration.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Blood oxygen levels are not the stimulus for ADH release.

toLevel2.stem: What is the effect of ADH on the collecting duct?

options.text: It increases the permeability of the collecting duct to water
It blocks water from entering the collecting duct
It increases filtration at the glomerulus
It stimulates the secretion of urea

explanations.a: Correct. ADH makes the collecting duct more permeable to water, allowing water to be reabsorbed by osmosis back into the blood.
explanations.b: Incorrect. ADH promotes water movement through the collecting duct wall, not blocking it.
explanations.c: Incorrect. ADH acts on the distal tubule and collecting duct, not on the glomerulus.
explanations.d: Incorrect. ADH regulates water permeability, not urea secretion.

toLevel2.stem: ADH is released when blood osmolality rises, such as during dehydration.

distractor.explanation: This statement is true. When the body is dehydrated, blood solute concentration (osmolality) increases, which triggers ADH release from the posterior pituitary.

toLevel2.stem: ADH acts on the proximal tubule to reabsorb glucose.

distractor.explanation: ADH acts on the distal tubule and collecting duct to increase water permeability. Glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubule is not controlled by ADH.

toLevel2.stem: ADH is released from the {{blank:1}} when blood osmolality rises.
ADH increases the water permeability of the {{blank:1}} and {{blank:2}}, allowing more water to be reabsorbed.
The regulation of water balance in the body is called {{blank:1}}.

toLevel3.stem: Why does ADH cause the production of more concentrated urine?

options.text: Because it increases water reabsorption from the collecting duct, leaving less water in the urine so waste is more concentrated
Because it increases the amount of urea secreted into the collecting duct
Because it increases blood pressure at the glomerulus, filtering more waste
Because it reduces the volume of blood flowing to the kidneys

explanations.a: Correct. ADH allows more water to move out of the collecting duct by osmosis. With less water remaining, the urine that forms is more concentrated with waste products like urea.
explanations.b: Incorrect. ADH does not control urea secretion. It specifically increases water permeability.
explanations.c: Incorrect. ADH acts on the tubule and collecting duct, not on glomerular blood pressure or filtration rate.
explanations.d: Incorrect. ADH does not reduce renal blood flow. It acts directly on the nephron's water permeability.

toLevel3.stem: How does ADH demonstrate a connection between the endocrine and excretory systems?

options.text: The endocrine system produces and releases ADH, which then acts on the excretory system's nephrons to regulate water balance
The excretory system produces ADH, which controls the endocrine system's hormone output
Both systems share the same organs and cannot function independently
ADH is produced in the kidney and acts on the pituitary gland

explanations.a: Correct. ADH is a hormone from the endocrine system (posterior pituitary) that targets cells in the nephron (excretory system), demonstrating how these two systems work together to maintain water homeostasis.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The excretory system does not produce ADH. ADH is produced by the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The endocrine and excretory systems have different organs but communicate through hormones like ADH.
explanations.d: Incorrect. ADH is released from the pituitary gland and acts on the kidney, not the other way around.

toLevel3.stem: Why does a person who has drunk a large volume of water produce more dilute urine?

options.text: Blood osmolality drops, so less ADH is released and less water is reabsorbed from the collecting duct
The kidneys filter more proteins, which dilutes the urine
The glomerulus stops filtering waste, so only water enters the tubule
ADH is released in large amounts to flush excess water out of the body

explanations.a: Correct. When blood is diluted by excess water, osmolality falls and ADH release decreases. Without ADH, the collecting duct remains less permeable to water, so more water stays in the filtrate and is excreted as dilute urine.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Proteins are not filtered and do not affect urine dilution.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The glomerulus continues filtering all small solutes regardless of hydration status.
explanations.d: Incorrect. ADH promotes water retention, not water excretion. Less ADH is released when the body is overhydrated.

toLevel3.stem: How does negative feedback operate in ADH regulation of water balance?

options.text: ADH promotes water reabsorption, which lowers blood osmolality, which in turn reduces ADH release
ADH release increases continuously until all water is reabsorbed from the filtrate
The kidneys signal the pituitary to produce more ADH as water is reabsorbed
Negative feedback prevents ADH from ever being released

explanations.a: Correct. As ADH causes water reabsorption, blood becomes more dilute (lower osmolality). This reduced osmolality signals the posterior pituitary to release less ADH, preventing over-correction.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Without negative feedback limiting it, ADH would over-correct. The system self-regulates to maintain balance.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The kidneys respond to ADH but do not signal the pituitary to increase its release. The stimulus is blood osmolality detected by the hypothalamus.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Negative feedback modulates ADH release; it does not prevent it entirely.

toLevel3.stem: Why is ADH described as an 'antidiuretic' hormone?

options.text: Because it works against diuresis (the production of large volumes of dilute urine) by promoting water reabsorption
Because it stimulates the kidneys to produce more urine
Because it prevents all urine production
Because it breaks down urea in the collecting duct

explanations.a: Correct. 'Anti-' means against and 'diuretic' refers to increased urine production. ADH reduces urine volume by promoting water reabsorption, working against dilute urine production.
explanations.b: Incorrect. ADH reduces urine production by increasing water reabsorption, not increasing it.
explanations.c: Incorrect. ADH reduces but does not completely prevent urine production. Some urine is always formed.
explanations.d: Incorrect. ADH does not break down urea; it controls water permeability of the tubule and collecting duct.

toLevel3.stem: By what mechanism does water move from the collecting duct into the blood when ADH is present?

options.text: Osmosis, because the surrounding medulla has a higher solute concentration than the filtrate
Active transport, because ADH provides the energy for water movement
Filtration, because ADH increases blood pressure
Diffusion of solutes, which carries water with them

explanations.a: Correct. ADH makes the walls permeable to water. Water then moves by osmosis from the dilute filtrate into the more concentrated surrounding tissue and blood.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Water moves by osmosis (passive), not active transport. ADH opens water channels but does not provide energy for water movement.
explanations.c: Incorrect. ADH does not increase blood pressure at this site. It changes the permeability of the tubule wall.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Water moves independently by osmosis through water channels; it is not carried by solute diffusion.

toLevel3.stem: When ADH levels are high, the collecting duct becomes more permeable to water, resulting in a smaller volume of more concentrated urine.

distractor.explanation: This is true. High ADH increases water channel insertion in the collecting duct, allowing more water to leave by osmosis. Less water in the filtrate means smaller urine volume and higher concentration.

toLevel3.stem: When blood osmolality rises, ADH release {{blank:1}}, causing more water to be reabsorbed and urine to become more {{blank:2}}.
ADH regulation is an example of {{blank:1}} feedback because the response (water reabsorption) reverses the original stimulus (high blood osmolality).
Water moves from the collecting duct into the blood by {{blank:1}} when ADH makes the walls permeable.

toLevel4.stem: After running 10 km without drinking, a person's urine is dark yellow and low in volume. Which sequence of events explains this?

options.text: Dehydration → blood osmolality rises → posterior pituitary releases more ADH → collecting duct becomes more permeable → more water reabsorbed → concentrated urine
Dehydration → kidneys produce more urea → urine becomes darker due to excess urea
Dehydration → glomerular filtration stops → no urine is formed
Dehydration → ADH release decreases → collecting duct expels more water → concentrated urine

explanations.a: Correct. Dehydration raises blood solute concentration, triggering ADH release. ADH increases water permeability of the collecting duct, more water is reabsorbed, and the remaining urine is small in volume and concentrated.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Urea production is determined by protein metabolism in the liver, not dehydration. Dark urine colour reflects concentration of all waste, not just urea.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Glomerular filtration continues during dehydration, though at a reduced rate. Urine is still produced.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Dehydration causes ADH release to increase, not decrease.

toLevel4.stem: A patient has a condition where their posterior pituitary cannot release ADH. What would you predict about their urine output?

options.text: They would produce large volumes of dilute urine because the collecting duct cannot increase its water permeability
They would produce no urine because ADH is needed for filtration
Their urine would be highly concentrated because water cannot be reabsorbed anywhere
Their urine output would be normal because other hormones fully compensate

explanations.a: Correct. Without ADH, the collecting duct remains relatively impermeable to water. Water stays in the filtrate and is excreted as large volumes of dilute urine. This condition is called diabetes insipidus.
explanations.b: Incorrect. ADH is not required for filtration. Filtration is driven by blood pressure at the glomerulus and proceeds independently of ADH.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Without ADH, less water is reabsorbed, so urine would be dilute, not concentrated.
explanations.d: Incorrect. While other mechanisms exist, they cannot fully compensate for the absence of ADH in regulating water reabsorption in the collecting duct.

toLevel4.stem: A person drinks 2 litres of water in a short period. Predict the sequence of events involving ADH.

options.text: Blood osmolality decreases → ADH release decreases → collecting duct less permeable to water → more dilute urine produced
Blood osmolality increases → ADH release increases → collecting duct reabsorbs more water
Blood volume increases → ADH release increases → urine becomes concentrated
Blood osmolality decreases → ADH release increases → kidneys excrete more ions

explanations.a: Correct. Excess water dilutes the blood, lowering osmolality. This reduces ADH release, so the collecting duct stays less permeable and more water passes through as dilute urine.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Drinking water lowers blood osmolality, which decreases (not increases) ADH release.
explanations.c: Incorrect. While blood volume increases, the key response is decreased ADH and dilute urine, not concentrated urine.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Decreased osmolality reduces ADH release; it does not increase it.

toLevel4.stem: Alcohol inhibits ADH release. What effect would drinking alcohol have on urine production?

options.text: Urine volume would increase and become more dilute because less water is reabsorbed in the collecting duct
Urine volume would decrease because the kidneys shut down
Urine would become more concentrated because alcohol dehydrates the body
Urine production would stop until alcohol is metabolised

explanations.a: Correct. By inhibiting ADH release, alcohol prevents the collecting duct from becoming permeable to water. More water remains in the filtrate and is excreted as dilute urine, contributing to dehydration.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The kidneys continue functioning; in fact, they produce more urine when ADH is suppressed.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Alcohol causes dehydration as a consequence of producing more dilute urine, not by concentrating it.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Urine production increases, not stops, when ADH is inhibited.

toLevel4.stem: If the medullary concentration gradient were disrupted (e.g. by a drug blocking ion transport in the ascending limb), how would this affect ADH's ability to concentrate urine?

options.text: Even with ADH present, less water would be reabsorbed because there is no osmotic gradient to drive water out of the collecting duct
ADH would increase the gradient to compensate
ADH would switch to active transport of water instead of relying on osmosis
The kidneys would stop producing urine entirely

explanations.a: Correct. ADH opens water channels, but water still moves by osmosis. If the medullary gradient is reduced (because the ascending limb is not pumping ions), there is less osmotic pull for water, so even with ADH, urine remains dilute.
explanations.b: Incorrect. ADH controls water permeability of the collecting duct; it does not create the medullary concentration gradient.
explanations.c: Incorrect. ADH facilitates osmosis through water channels. It cannot switch to active transport of water.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The kidneys would still produce urine, but it would be more dilute than normal.

toLevel4.stem: A blood test shows normal ADH levels but a patient is still producing large volumes of dilute urine. What could explain this?

options.text: The target cells in the collecting duct may lack functional ADH receptors, so they cannot respond to the hormone
The glomerulus is filtering too much protein
The proximal tubule is reabsorbing too much glucose
The posterior pituitary is releasing too much ADH

explanations.a: Correct. If ADH receptors on collecting duct cells are non-functional, the cells cannot respond to ADH even when it is present. This is called nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Proteins are not normally filtered. This would indicate glomerular damage, not an ADH-related issue.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubule is unrelated to ADH function or water balance in the collecting duct.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The question states ADH levels are normal, not elevated.

toLevel4.stem: During a hot day, a person sweats heavily and does not drink water. Trace the expected change in their blood osmolality and urine colour.

options.text: Blood osmolality rises, ADH increases, more water is reabsorbed, and urine becomes darker yellow
Blood osmolality drops, ADH decreases, and urine becomes pale
Blood osmolality stays the same because sweat contains no water
Blood osmolality rises, ADH decreases, and urine volume increases

explanations.a: Correct. Sweating loses water, raising blood osmolality. This triggers more ADH release, increasing water reabsorption. Less water in the urine means waste is more concentrated, producing darker urine.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Losing water through sweat increases blood osmolality, it does not decrease it.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Sweat is primarily water with dissolved salts, so heavy sweating significantly reduces body water.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Rising osmolality triggers more ADH, which decreases urine volume, not increases it.

toLevel4.stem: Alcohol inhibits {{blank:1}} release, causing the collecting duct to remain less permeable and producing {{blank:2}} volumes of dilute urine.
If a patient's collecting duct cells lack functional ADH {{blank:1}}, they cannot respond to the hormone even when it is present in the blood.
After drinking 2 litres of water, blood osmolality {{blank:1}} and ADH release {{blank:2}}, producing dilute urine.

toLevel5.stem: A student claims: 'ADH directly moves water from the collecting duct into the blood.' Evaluate this statement.

options.text: It is inaccurate because ADH increases the permeability of the collecting duct wall; water then moves passively by osmosis down its concentration gradient
It is correct because ADH provides energy for water transport
It is correct because ADH binds to water molecules and carries them across the membrane
It is inaccurate because ADH acts on the glomerulus, not the collecting duct

explanations.a: Correct. ADH's role is to open water channels (aquaporins) in the collecting duct wall. Water then moves passively by osmosis due to the concentration gradient between the dilute filtrate and the concentrated medullary tissue. ADH does not directly transport water.
explanations.b: Incorrect. ADH does not provide energy for water transport. Water moves by osmosis, a passive process.
explanations.c: Incorrect. ADH does not bind to or carry water molecules. It binds to receptors on collecting duct cells to trigger water channel insertion.
explanations.d: Incorrect. ADH does act on the collecting duct (and distal tubule), not the glomerulus.

toLevel5.stem: Analyse why the ADH system is considered a negative feedback loop rather than a positive feedback loop.

options.text: Because the response (water reabsorption lowering blood osmolality) opposes the original stimulus (high blood osmolality), reducing ADH release
Because ADH release always increases over time
Because the response amplifies the stimulus, causing more ADH to be released
Because the pituitary gland inhibits the kidney from responding

explanations.a: Correct. In negative feedback, the output reverses the input. High osmolality triggers ADH → water reabsorption → osmolality falls → ADH release decreases. The system self-corrects toward a set point.
explanations.b: Incorrect. In negative feedback, ADH release adjusts up or down depending on conditions; it does not always increase.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Amplification of the stimulus is characteristic of positive feedback, not negative feedback.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The pituitary does not inhibit the kidney; it communicates via ADH, and the kidney responds accordingly.

toLevel5.stem: Compare the consequences of having no ADH production versus having non-functional ADH receptors on collecting duct cells.

options.text: Both produce similar symptoms (excessive dilute urine), but the causes differ: one is an endocrine deficiency and the other is a receptor defect in the excretory system
No ADH production causes concentrated urine; non-functional receptors cause dilute urine
Non-functional receptors would have no effect because other receptors can compensate
No ADH production would stop urine production entirely

explanations.a: Correct. Both conditions result in the collecting duct being unable to reabsorb water effectively, producing large volumes of dilute urine. The first (central diabetes insipidus) is an endocrine problem; the second (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus) is a kidney receptor problem.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Both conditions produce dilute urine, not one producing concentrated and the other dilute.
explanations.c: Incorrect. ADH receptors are specific; other receptors cannot substitute for their function in water permeability regulation.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Urine production continues even without ADH; it simply becomes more dilute and voluminous.

toLevel5.stem: Evaluate whether ADH alone is sufficient to maintain water balance in the body.

options.text: No, because ADH can only increase water reabsorption from existing filtrate; overall water balance also depends on water intake, sweat loss, and other hormonal controls
Yes, because ADH controls all water movement in the body
Yes, because ADH can produce water when the body is dehydrated
No, because ADH only works when a person is overhydrated

explanations.a: Correct. ADH adjusts how much water the kidney retains, but total water balance also depends on drinking, sweating, breathing, and other hormones like aldosterone. ADH is one component of a broader homeostatic system.
explanations.b: Incorrect. ADH specifically controls water permeability of the distal tubule and collecting duct. It does not control water movement throughout the entire body.
explanations.c: Incorrect. ADH cannot create water. It can only recover water from filtrate that has already been produced.
explanations.d: Incorrect. ADH is most active during dehydration (high osmolality), not only during overhydration.

toLevel5.stem: Analyse why ADH targets the collecting duct and distal tubule specifically, rather than the proximal tubule where most reabsorption occurs.

options.text: The proximal tubule handles obligatory bulk reabsorption, while the distal tubule and collecting duct provide adjustable, fine-tuned water recovery based on the body's needs
The proximal tubule is too far from the medulla for ADH to reach it
ADH cannot cross the cortex where the proximal tubule is located
The proximal tubule already reabsorbs all water, leaving nothing for ADH to act on

explanations.a: Correct. The proximal tubule consistently reabsorbs ~65% of water regardless of conditions. The distal tubule and collecting duct are where the body can adjust water reabsorption via ADH to respond to changing hydration needs.
explanations.b: Incorrect. ADH travels through the bloodstream and reaches all parts of the nephron. The proximal tubule simply lacks ADH receptors for water regulation.
explanations.c: Incorrect. ADH circulates in the blood throughout the kidney. The difference is in receptor expression, not hormone access.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The proximal tubule reabsorbs 65% of water, not all of it. Significant water remains for adjustment later.

toLevel5.stem: A student argues: 'Caffeine and alcohol both increase urine output, so they must work the same way as reducing ADH.' Evaluate this reasoning.

options.text: The conclusion about increased output may be correct for alcohol (which inhibits ADH), but caffeine's mechanism is different, so the reasoning is oversimplified
The reasoning is correct because all diuretics work by reducing ADH
The reasoning is incorrect because neither caffeine nor alcohol affects urine output
The reasoning is correct because both substances are processed identically by the kidney

explanations.a: Correct. Alcohol does inhibit ADH release, directly reducing water reabsorption. However, caffeine increases urine output through different mechanisms (e.g. increasing blood flow to the kidney). Having the same outcome does not mean the same mechanism.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Diuretics can work through multiple mechanisms, including increasing filtration rate, blocking ion reabsorption, or inhibiting ADH. Not all work via ADH.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Both caffeine and alcohol do increase urine output, but through different pathways.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Caffeine and alcohol have different chemical properties and are processed differently by the body.

toLevel5.stem: How does the ADH feedback loop illustrate the interdependence of the endocrine and excretory systems?

options.text: The endocrine system detects osmolality changes and releases ADH, while the excretory system executes the response; neither system can maintain water balance independently
The excretory system produces ADH and the endocrine system filters the blood
Both systems detect osmolality independently and respond without communicating
The endocrine system only activates if the excretory system fails completely

explanations.a: Correct. The hypothalamus (part of the endocrine/nervous system) detects blood osmolality and the posterior pituitary releases ADH. The kidney's nephrons respond by adjusting water reabsorption. This cross-system communication is essential for homeostasis.
explanations.b: Incorrect. ADH is produced by the hypothalamus and released by the posterior pituitary (endocrine system). The kidneys filter blood (excretory system).
explanations.c: Incorrect. The systems communicate via ADH in the bloodstream; they do not operate independently.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The endocrine system continuously regulates ADH based on blood osmolality, not only during system failure.

toLevel5.stem: A researcher proposes treating dehydration by administering synthetic ADH. Evaluate the limitations of this approach.

options.text: ADH can only recover water already in the filtrate; if body water is severely depleted, there is insufficient filtrate water to reabsorb, so fluid intake is still essential
There are no limitations because ADH will fully restore water balance
The limitation is that synthetic ADH cannot reach the kidneys
ADH would cause the kidneys to produce more urine, worsening dehydration

explanations.a: Correct. ADH maximises water recovery from filtrate, but if the body is severely dehydrated, blood volume and filtrate production are both reduced. ADH cannot create new water; oral or intravenous fluids are necessary to replace lost water.
explanations.b: Incorrect. ADH has limits; it can only retain water from existing filtrate and cannot replace water that has already been lost.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Synthetic ADH can be administered and reaches the kidneys via the bloodstream, just like natural ADH.
explanations.d: Incorrect. ADH reduces urine output by promoting water reabsorption, not increasing it.

toLevel5.stem: ADH regulation is a negative feedback loop because the response ({{blank:1}} blood osmolality) opposes the original stimulus ({{blank:2}} blood osmolality).

Both central and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus produce dilute urine, but central is caused by a deficiency in ADH {{blank:1}} while nephrogenic is caused by defective {{blank:2}} on collecting duct cells.
